original_reason: Crown dome and brim are one rigid piece of this bowler hat, so the hand explicitly holding the brim 'against rotation' cancels the very rotation the other hand applies to the dome.

Hand B's hold on the lower hemisphere sits directly beneath hand A's downward push, so the upward support cancels the push and the ball is clamped between the palms instead of being driven toward the floor.
Rim and mid-height wall are the same rigid pot, so hand B's stated job of stabilizing the body against rotation directly resists the rotation hand A must produce to invert it.
Inverting turns the whole terracotta pot including its base, so the hand told to hold the base still against that rotation is anchoring a part that must travel, cancelling the actuating hand.
Both contacts are on the same one-piece bowl wall, so a hand stabilizing the object against rotation opposes the 180-degree inversion the opposite hand is supposed to drive.
The handle is rigidly fixed to the box, so turning it turns the whole body, and the hand holding the opposite side wall against rotation resists exactly that motion.
The carrot is one rigid cone, so hand B holding the upper body 'against rotation' directly cancels hand A's rotation at mid-height of the same rigid body.

The render shows one solid moulded piece - large hollow hub and small boss joined by a rigid arm with no joint between them - so the hand clamping the large cylinder cancels exactly the torque the other hand applies at the small mount and nothing can turn relative to anything.

On a smooth ball needing no balancing, the hand gripping the lower hemisphere to 'stabilize against sliding' directly cancels the upper-hemisphere hand's translating push and pins the ground-contact region so it cannot roll.

The render is one plain rigid annulus with no hub or axle, so the hand gripping the inner edge of the central opening to stabilize against rotation resists the very torque the other hand applies to the outer wall of that same body.
The dark metal blade is seated rigidly in the wooden shaft that carries the crossbar and end knob, so holding that shaft 'against rotation' locks the very rod the other hand is trying to twist.

The object is a finned downlight housing whose side straps are hinged spring clips fixed to that same housing, so the hand clamping the mid-height cylinder wall blocks the rotation the strap hand is supposed to drive.

The scan is a single rubber tire carcass with no wheel or hub inside, so the hand holding the inner wall of the hollow interior to stabilize it opposes the hand rotating the outer sidewall of the same rigid piece.

Hand B clamps the side walls of two opposite lobes to 'stabilize the body against rotation', which locks the very rotation the task asks for, and on this three-lobe spinner the center knob is the fixed race, so hand A's torque is cancelled by hand B's grip.
